body.x: If you have come across the word mut'ah — in a family argument, a documentary, or a conversation with a Shia friend — you may have found the explanations either very technical or very heated. This page takes a third route: plain words, no shouting. It explains what mut'ah is in Twelver Shia Islam, why it exists there, how it works and how it ends. It is written for the curious — including readers who are not Shia at all, and families trying to understand something a prospective in-law has mentioned.

Mut'ah is an Arabic word connected to enjoyment or benefit, and in this context it names a marriage contract made for a fixed, agreed period of time. That is the whole idea in one sentence. An ordinary nikah is open-ended: entered into for life, and ended only by divorce or death. A mut'ah is a marriage whose length is written into the contract from the start, whether that length is months or years. When the time runs out, the marriage is over by itself. Nothing needs to be filed, pronounced or argued about; the contract simply reaches the end the couple agreed at the beginning.
Why does it exist in Shia thought?

Shia scholars hold that this form of marriage was permitted in the time of the Prophet Muhammad and was never withdrawn by the Quran; their reading of the verse in Surah an-Nisa that speaks of giving women their due in such arrangements is the foundation of the ruling. Sunni scholars read the history differently and hold that it was prohibited, which is why mut'ah exists in Shia law and not in Sunni law — a genuine, centuries-old difference of interpretation, not a misunderstanding a webpage can tidy away. Within Shia thought, the reasoning usually given is pastoral: people sometimes face circumstances — long travel, study far from home, a lengthy engagement in a society where dating is not an option — where the tradition prefers a defined, honest contract with known rights over secrecy or pretence. Whether one finds that reasoning persuasive is a matter of conviction. The point here is narrower: in Twelver fiqh, mut'ah is a real contract with real rules, not a loophole.
So how does it actually work?

Think of it as a nikah with two extra sentences. As in a permanent marriage, there is a spoken contract — the offer and acceptance, in Arabic, said by the couple themselves or by representatives they appoint. As in a permanent marriage, a mahr is named: something of value that belongs to the wife. The differences are the two that define it. The length of the marriage must be stated and agreed; if it is not, Shia jurists generally treat the contract as a permanent one. And the mahr cannot be left vague — in a mut'ah, an unspecified mahr undoes the contract altogether. The permissions that guard a permanent nikah guard this one too: a woman who has not been married before will, under the majority of marjas, need her father's or paternal grandfather's permission, exactly as she would otherwise. Details vary between marjas, and anyone actually facing this question should confirm them with their own.

What the contract does not automatically carry is worth knowing. Unless the couple writes it in as a condition, a wife in a mut'ah does not have the automatic claim to maintenance that a permanent wife has, and the two do not automatically inherit from one another. Conditions can be added — couples do stipulate things like financial support, or that the marriage will not be consummated — and once stipulated, those conditions bind. There is no divorce in a mut'ah, because there is nothing to dissolve: the husband may gift back the remaining time to end it early, or the couple simply let it expire.

Two protections follow a mut'ah, and they are not optional extras. If a child is born from it, that child is fully legitimate in Shia law: the child of a married couple, with the same rights of name, lineage and inheritance from both parents as any other child. And when a mut'ah ends, the woman observes an iddah, a waiting period — in general terms, two menstrual cycles, or forty-five days for a woman who does not menstruate — before she may enter another marriage; if she is pregnant, it runs until the birth. These rules exist for the same reasons they exist after a permanent marriage: clarity about lineage, and dignity for everyone involved.
An honest word about sensitivities — and about this site

It would be dishonest to pretend mut'ah is uncontroversial even among Shia families. Many regard it as a legitimate but rarely fitting provision; some communities barely discuss it; others worry, not unreasonably, about its misuse by people who want the label of marriage without its responsibilities. Scholars who permit it generally surround it with the very conditions described above, precisely so that it cannot be casual. If the subject matters to your own situation, the right next step is not a website at all — it is a question to your own marja, whose ruling is the one that binds you.

One clarification belongs on this page. Shia Rishta exists for permanent nikah only: every profile on the platform — free to use, with photo privacy controls and messaging that opens only on mutual interest — is there to find a spouse for life. This explainer exists because families deserve clear information, not because the service offers anything else. Understanding a ruling and choosing it are different things. Our part is simply to make sure the understanding is accurate.

excerpt: Mut'ah in plain words: what a fixed-term marriage contract is in Twelver Shia Islam, why it exists there, how it works and ends, what it means for children — and why Shia Rishta is for permanent nikah only.
title: Mutah (temporary marriage) in Shia Islam: explained simply
